material_errors.description: The eastern Seleucid realm is wrongly partitioned into a fictitious separate 'Kingdom of the Satraps' and an independent Bactria, although Bactria did not secede until the mid-third century BCE.

summary: The principal western successor kingdoms are mapped clearly, but the invented eastern political partition requires one material correction.

material_errors.description: The Palmyrene Empire is drawn without its major Egyptian possession and most of its Asia Minor reach around 271, materially shrinking a principal breakaway state.
A separate Kingdom of Odaenathus dated 260-267 is presented as a simultaneous polity in 271 even though the Palmyrene regime succeeded his authority after his death.

summary: The map is polished and complete in form, but it both truncates Palmyrene control and revives a defunct overlapping polity.
A strong and readable war map whose occupation and campaign layers are somewhat schematic but do not create a material historical error.

material_errors.description: The late-750 Abbasid control fill is confined essentially to Sindh while Khurasan, Iraq, Syria, and nearly the entire overthrown caliphate remain colored Umayyad, reversing the requested transition's central political geography.
Tahirid semi-autonomy is dated from 748 and mapped as contemporary, although Tahirid rule in Khurasan began in 821.
Baghdad is symbolized as the Abbasid capital in 750 even while the map acknowledges that the city was founded only in 762.
Al-Andalus is presented as a separate Umayyad emirate in 750, before Abd al-Rahman established that emirate in 756.

summary: Arrows and chronology cannot rescue a map whose control layer depicts the Umayyads as still ruling nearly everything and compounds that reversal with several major anachronisms.

material_errors.description: The steppe layer presents extinct Eastern and Western Turkic khaganates as contemporary powers around 750; the Second Turkic Khaganate ended in 744 and the Western Turkic realm had fallen much earlier, while the Uyghurs were the relevant successor power.

summary: Routes and regional coverage are excellent, but one systemic anachronism misstates the principal steppe order in 750.

material_errors.description: Central and eastern Java around 900 are given the wrong political identity: the map substitutes the later Janggala/Kahuripan order for the period's Medang or Mataram realm.

summary: The maritime network, ports, and straits are unusually effective, but Java's principal political layer is displaced by an eleventh-century successor order.

material_errors.description: The White Horde is identified as the 'Orda of Sibir,' conflating Orda's eastern Jochid ulus with a distinct Siberian formation and misnaming a principal Mongol successor.

summary: The continental khanate, route, and city structure is useful, but the White Horde's political identity requires a material correction.

material_errors.description: Cahokia and the Mississippian chiefdom complex are moved from the Mississippi Valley to southern Brazil and Paraguay, a transcontinental placement error.
The Plains are described as pre-contact horse cultures and include the Comanche in 1491, imposing a post-contact equestrian political order on the requested date.
Tiwanaku is presented as a contemporary major center in 1491 although its urban polity had collapsed centuries earlier.

summary: Broad continental coverage and attractive rendering are undermined by a transcontinental Mississippian error and multiple period-defining anachronisms.

material_errors.description: Saint-Louis is shown as a European fort or factory in 1590 although the French settlement was founded in 1659.
Dahomey is mapped as an established kingdom in 1590 despite arising only in the early seventeenth century.

The coastal political layer invents or territorializes entities such as a unified Kingdom of Sierra Leone and Portuguese Senegambia rather than representing the period's actual polities and limited European footholds.

summary: Songhai, the Niger, trade routes, and invasion corridor are well drawn, but the wider coastal context contains several independent chronological and political fabrications.

material_errors.description: The Mughal fill absorbs nearly the entire Deccan and southern peninsula around 1600, erasing still-independent powers including Bijapur and Golconda and grossly overstating Mughal control.
Egypt is assigned to a surviving Mamluk Sultanate in 1600 even though the Ottomans ended that sultanate and incorporated Egypt in 1517.
The map presents the later Dzungar and Kokand khanates as contemporary neighbors around 1600, although they emerged in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries respectively.
A broad Safavid-influence zone is drawn across North Africa, far outside any credible Safavid frontier or contested borderland.

summary: Two imperial footprints and several neighboring-state claims are wrong enough that the otherwise excellent drawing fails as a political map of 1600.

material_errors.description: Portugal is marked as an independence recognized or confirmed by the Peace of Westphalia, although Spain recognized Portuguese independence only in 1668 and the 1648 settlement did not establish it.

summary: The HRE, principal states, and recognized Dutch and Swiss outcomes are clear, but the prominent Portuguese settlement claim is materially false.

material_errors.description: The Indian theater divides and fills almost the whole subcontinent as British India or French India, vastly overstating both companies' territorial control during the war.
The European chronology says Russia withdrew in 1760-1761 under Empress Elizabeth, although Russia made peace with Prussia in 1762 under Peter III after Elizabeth's death.

summary: The global theater structure is impressively complete, but a grossly false Indian control map and a central European chronology error require independent corrections.

material_errors.description: Egypt is encoded as Italian effective control instead of a Khedivate under British occupation, contradicting the map's central control-versus-claim distinction.
The Congo Free State is encoded as French effective control and described as a Belgian association rather than Leopold II's separately recognized Congo state.
Germany and its newly declared African colonial possessions or claims are absent from both the legend and map despite being indispensable to an Africa-in-1885 account.
Liberia, one of the principal independent African states in 1885, is omitted from the political layer.

summary: The map attempts the requested distinction, but misclassifies two defining cases and omits key colonial and independent actors, defeating its central purpose.

material_errors.description: The U.S. intervention zone is placed south of Manchuria near the Sea of Japan rather than around Vladivostok and the eastern Siberian rail corridor where American forces operated.
Yudenich is assigned to the Northern Front even though he commanded the Northwestern Army and its Petrograd offensive, conflating two principal White fronts.

summary: The control, rail, and campaign framework is strong, but one major intervention is misplaced and one principal White command is misidentified.

material_errors.description: Cuba is colored as a U.S. ally or partner in 1962 despite its close Soviet alignment and role as host of Soviet missiles.
Yugoslavia is assigned to the U.S.-aligned category instead of the non-aligned movement it helped lead.
Diego Garcia is listed as a British Indian Ocean Territory strategic base in 1962, although BIOT was created in 1965 and the joint base followed later.
The alliance account omits both SEATO and CENTO, two principal treaty systems active in 1962.

summary: The global layout and flashpoints are readable, but central alignment miscategorizations, an anachronistic base, and omitted treaty systems make the 1962 account misleading.
